title: Councils should abolish minimum parking requirements for new housing
oneLiner: Whether planning schemes should stop requiring a set number of car spaces per new dwelling and let builders decide.
body: Most Australian planning schemes require new apartments and townhouses to include a minimum number of off-street car spaces, typically one or more per dwelling. The proposal removes the minimum. Developers could still build parking; they would no longer be required to.
contextBackground:
Parking minimums date from the mid-twentieth century and were set to keep new buildings from pushing cars onto the street ([Wikipedia: parking mandates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parking_mandates)). They are now identified as a large hidden cost of housing: Grattan's May 2026 report [Wasted space](https://grattan.edu.au/report/wasted-space/) estimates they add roughly $70,000 to a two-bedroom apartment in Sydney, $62,000 in Melbourne and up to $137,000 in Perth, and that Australia builds more than a billion dollars of unused off-street parking a year.

Some Australian governments have moved. [Victoria removed minimums](https://www.premier.vic.gov.au/yes-more-homes-and-yes-more-local-infrastructure) near high-frequency public transport in December 2025, and New South Wales' low- and mid-rise housing rules limit councils' ability to refuse projects on parking grounds. Grattan wants states to override council minimums everywhere.
contextDisagreement: Both sides accept that parking is costly and that some residents will own cars regardless. They divide on who should bear the mismatch: the resident who parks on the street, the neighbour who loses a space, or the buyer who pays for a car space they do not use. Grattan's finding that up to 40 per cent of inner-Melbourne street spaces sit empty at night is the newest evidence in that fight, and no organised opposition to removal has yet made a public case.

timeline.label: 1950s–70s
timeline.text: Australian councils adopt parking minimums as cars become universal.
Shoup's work popularises the argument that minimums are an unpriced subsidy to driving.
Auckland removes minimums citywide; several US cities follow over the next decade.

timeline.label: Dec 2025
timeline.text: Victoria removes parking minimums for new homes near high-frequency public transport, citing 40 per cent empty residential car parks in inner Melbourne.

timeline.label: May 2026
timeline.text: Grattan Institute's 'Wasted space' calls on states to override council minimums nationally: 86,000 unneeded spaces and $5.2 billion over five years.

otherClaim.title: Parking minimums add roughly $70,000 to the cost of a two-bedroom apartment in Sydney, $62,000 in Melbourne and up to $137,000 in Perth

claimItself.title: Parking minimums add roughly $70,000 to the cost of a two-bedroom apartment in Sydney, $62,000 in Melbourne and up to $137,000 in Perth
claimItself.oneLiner: Grattan's 2026 estimates of what the rules add to each new apartment.
claimItself.body: Basement and podium parking is among the most expensive floor space in a building, and the requirement often forces an extra basement level. Grattan's May 2026 report put the cost of mandated parking at about $70,000 per two-bedroom apartment in Sydney, $62,000 in Melbourne, $113,000 in Brisbane, $95,000 in Adelaide and $137,000 in Perth, recovered in the price of every apartment including those bought by people without cars.

otherClaim.title: Auckland removed minimum parking requirements citywide in 2016, and new developments near frequent transit have since provided markedly less parking

claimItself.title: Auckland removed minimum parking requirements citywide in 2016, and new developments near frequent transit have since provided markedly less parking
claimItself.oneLiner: The closest large-scale natural experiment in a comparable city.
claimItself.body: The Auckland Unitary Plan, operative from late 2016, removed minimum parking requirements across the city. Subsequent research found that developments near frequent public transport built substantially fewer spaces per dwelling, while those in car-dependent areas continued to provide roughly what they had before.

otherClaim.title: New housing completions have not kept pace with population growth in Australia's largest cities over the past decade

claimItself.title: New housing completions have not kept pace with population growth in Australia's largest cities over the past decade
claimItself.oneLiner: Dwellings built per new resident have fallen, and vacancy rates in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Perth sit near record lows.
claimItself.body: Completions peaked around 2017 and fell through the pandemic as costs rose and builders failed, while population growth resumed at pace. The national housing agency's projections show a cumulative shortfall against household formation through the second half of the decade.

otherClaim.title: Developers still build parking where buyers want it; minimums only bind where demand is below the mandate

claimItself.title: Developers still build parking where buyers want it; minimums only bind where demand is below the mandate
claimItself.oneLiner: A minimum changes nothing where people want cars, and forces waste where they do not.
claimItself.body: In car-dependent suburbs, apartments without parking do not sell, so developers build it whether or not it is required. The minimum only has an effect where buyers would accept less parking than the rule demands, which is exactly where it is most costly and least useful.

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: Seventy-three per cent of Melbourne apartments built since 2019 provided exactly the legal minimum number of car spaces

claimItself.title: Victoria removed minimum parking requirements for new homes near high-frequency public transport in December 2025
claimItself.oneLiner: The first Australian state to act, on an accessibility basis.
claimItself.body: From December 2025 Victorian planning rules vary parking requirements by public-transport accessibility level, with no minimums in areas of high or medium accessibility. Accessible parking for people with disabilities is unchanged and developers may still build more spaces with a permit.

otherClaim.title: Without minimums, residents' cars spill onto surrounding streets and crowd out existing residents

claimItself.title: Without minimums, residents' cars spill onto surrounding streets and crowd out existing residents
claimItself.oneLiner: If the building does not house the cars, the street does.
claimItself.body: Residents of new developments will own cars at roughly the rate of their neighbours, whatever the building provides. Opponents of removal argue the predictable result is competition for kerbside space that existing residents regard as theirs.

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: Up to 40 per cent of residential and on-street parking in inner Melbourne sits empty at night, and most street spaces are used by residents who already have off-street parking

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: Councils can manage street parking with permits and pricing, independently of what new buildings provide

otherClaim.title: Most Australian suburbs lack public transport frequent enough to make living without a car practical

claimItself.title: Most Australian suburbs lack public transport frequent enough to make living without a car practical
claimItself.oneLiner: Outside the inner ring, a car is not a choice.
claimItself.body: Census journey-to-work data shows car use above 70 per cent in most middle and outer suburbs, and service frequency outside peak hours is low. In those areas the assumption behind removing minimums, that some residents will choose not to own a car, does not hold for most households.
